title: The Temple Finished and Dedicated
summary: Darius has the archives searched, and Cyrus's original memorandum authorizing the temple is found at Ecbatana. Darius confirms it, orders Tattenai to leave the work alone and to fund it from provincial taxes, and threatens anyone who interferes. The temple is completed in the sixth year of Darius, dedicated with joy and sacrifice, and the returned exiles, joined by others who had separated themselves from the uncleanness of the land, celebrate the Passover and the Feast of Unleavened Bread.
story: Chapter 5 left the builders at work and Tattenai's letter on its way to Darius. Chapter 6 gives the answer, and it is better than anyone could have hoped. The inquiry meant to check the Jews ends up confirming them, and the governor who questioned them is ordered to pay for the work. The story that began in chapter 1 with Cyrus's decree now reaches its goal: the house of God stands in Jerusalem again, about twenty-three years after the first return and about seventy years after Solomon's temple was burned. The chapter closes the first half of Ezra with worship, and the Hebrew narrative resumes at verse 19 with the Passover, the feast of Israel's first great deliverance. Chapter 7 will then jump ahead nearly sixty years to Ezra himself.
historical:
Ecbatana (modern Hamadan in western Iran) was the old capital of Media and a summer residence of the Persian kings. Cyrus is known to have spent time there, so it is a plausible place for a record from his first year to be kept. The memorandum found there (verses 3-5) reads like an archive note rather than a public proclamation: it specifies the size of the building, the method of construction, and royal funding, and it orders the return of the vessels.

Darius's decree fits what is known of his reign. His own inscription at Behistun, carved on a cliff in western Iran, describes how he punished rebels, including by impaling them, so the threat in verse 11 is not rhetorical exaggeration. The request that the Jews pray for the life of the king and his sons (verse 10) matches Persian practice; the Cyrus Cylinder likewise asks the gods Cyrus restored to intercede daily for him and his son. The temple was finished on the third day of Adar in Darius's sixth year, which corresponds to early 515 BC. The Passover followed in the first month of the new year, a few weeks later. Artaxerxes is mentioned in verse 14 although he reigned later (465-424 BC); the writer probably includes him because his support for the temple is described in chapter 7.
cultural:
The dedication of a temple was a public ceremony that marked the building as the dwelling of a god and inaugurated its worship. The sacrifices here (a hundred bulls, two hundred rams, four hundred lambs, and twelve goats) are modest compared with Solomon's dedication, where the offerings ran to tens of thousands (1 Kings 8:63), a reminder of how small and poor the community was. The twelve goats, one for each tribe of Israel, show that the returnees, though mostly from Judah and Benjamin, saw themselves as representing the whole people of Israel.

Passover, kept on the fourteenth day of the first month, remembered the night when God spared Israel's firstborn and brought them out of Egypt (Exodus 12). It was followed by the seven-day Feast of Unleavened Bread. Only those who were ritually clean could eat it, so the priests and Levites purified themselves first. Verse 21 is significant: those who had separated themselves from the uncleanness of the peoples of the land to seek the LORD joined the returned exiles at the meal. This was the old provision for outsiders who committed themselves to Israel's God (Exodus 12:48), and it shows that the community's boundary was religious commitment, not birth alone.
literary: The chapter falls into two parts in two languages. Verses 1-18, still in Aramaic, contain the rediscovered memorandum of Cyrus (3-5), Darius's decree (6-12), and the report of its execution, the temple's completion, and its dedication (13-18). At verse 19 the text returns to Hebrew for the Passover. The decree deliberately echoes the language of Tattenai's letter in chapter 5, and the phrase the house of God recurs throughout like a drumbeat. The chapter ends on joy: the people keep the feast with joy because the LORD had made them joyful, and turned the heart of the king toward them. The mention of the king of Assyria in verse 22, applied to the Persian ruler of the old Assyrian lands, reminds the reader of the empire that had first scattered Israel and now, in a sense, helps restore it.

outline.t: Darius's decree: leave the work alone and pay for it
The temple completed in Darius's sixth year
The dedication of the house of God
The Passover and the Feast of Unleavened Bread

doctrines.note: An inquiry meant to stop the work ends with the empire funding it. The chapter credits the result to the LORD, who turned the heart of the king (verse 22), showing God's rule over the decisions of rulers without overriding their ordinary processes.

The builders prosper through the prophesying of Haggai and Zechariah and finish according to the command of the God of Israel as well as the decrees of the kings (verse 14). God's word and the kings' decrees run together, but God's command comes first.

The Passover recalls God's rescue of Israel from Egypt, and the returned exiles keep it as people rescued again from Babylon. Those who separated themselves from impurity to seek the LORD share the meal, showing that deliverance is received by turning to God.

The Passover was a covenant meal that joined Israel's present generation to God's past deliverance. Keeping it immediately after the dedication shows the community renewing its identity through the ordinance God gave.

words.note: Chanukkah, dedication, in Aramaic in verses 16 and 17. The same word in Hebrew names the dedication of the altar in Numbers 7 and at Solomon's temple (2 Chronicles 7:9), and it later gave its name to the Jewish festival of Hanukkah, which remembers the rededication of this same temple in 164 BC after its desecration under Antiochus IV.

Badal, to separate or divide, the verb used in Genesis 1 for God separating light from darkness. In verse 21 it describes those who separated themselves from the uncleanness of the land to seek the LORD. Separation here is not withdrawal from people as such but turning from impurity and false worship toward God, and it will become a key word in chapters 9 and 10.

Pesach, Passover, from a verb meaning to pass over or spare, recalling that God passed over the houses marked with blood (Exodus 12:13). Celebrating it just after the temple's completion presents the return from Babylon as a second exodus, another rescue from bondage.

christ: The chapter ends with a restored temple and a Passover meal, and both are central images in the New Testament's account of Jesus. This temple, later expanded by Herod, is the one Jesus taught in and cleansed, and whose destruction he predicted (Mark 13:1-2). John records Jesus speaking of his own body as the temple that would be destroyed and raised in three days (John 2:19-21), presenting him as the true place where God dwells with his people. At Passover Jesus shared his last meal with his disciples and gave the bread and cup new meaning in his coming death (Luke 22:14-20), and Paul calls Christ our Passover lamb (1 Corinthians 5:7). The link is not that Ezra 6 hides a prophecy of Jesus, but that the institutions it restores, temple and Passover, are the very ones the New Testament says Jesus fulfills.
questions: The inquiry that might have ended the work instead confirmed and funded it. Can you recall a situation where something you feared turned out to serve a good purpose?
The first thing the community did with its finished temple was worship and celebrate a meal of remembrance. How does remembering God's past rescues shape the way you receive present blessings?
Outsiders who turned to seek the LORD shared the Passover with the returned exiles. What does this suggest about how communities of faith should draw their boundaries?
